misconception.description: building lifetime value on the revenue a customer pays rather than on the gross margin the company keeps, which overstates the value by the whole cost of serving the customer

worked_example.text: A gym charges EUR 40 a month. Staffing, cleaning and equipment wear cost it 30% of that, leaving a 70% gross margin, and 7% of members cancel each month.
worked_example.solution: Margin per member per month = 40 x 0.7 = EUR 28. The average member stays 1 / 0.07 months. Lifetime value = 28 / 0.07 = EUR 400.

problem.text: A software company charges EUR 60 per customer per month. Its gross margin is 75% of that revenue, and 5% of its customers cancel each month. What is the lifetime value of a customer, before discounting?

distractors.note: the documented misconception: using revenue rather than the gross margin the company keeps
assuming a fixed one-year life instead of deriving the expected life from the churn rate

hints: Lifetime value has two ingredients: what the company keeps from a customer each month, and how many months the customer stays. Work out each one before combining them.
The company does not keep the whole subscription fee. Apply the gross margin to the monthly revenue first, so that the cost of serving the customer is already taken out.
A monthly cancellation rate implies an average life of one divided by that rate. Dividing the monthly margin by the churn rate gives the same result in one step.
worked_solution: Step 1: find the monthly gross margin per customer: 60 x 0.75 = EUR 45. This is what the company keeps after the cost of serving the customer. Step 2: find the expected life: if 5% cancel each month, a customer stays 1 / 0.05 = 20 months on average. Step 3: multiply: 45 x 20 = EUR 900, which is the same as dividing the monthly margin by the churn rate. Using the full EUR 60 of revenue instead would give EUR 1,200 and would credit the customer with money that is spent on serving them.

near_transfer.text: The same software company, still charging EUR 60 a month at a 75% gross margin, improves its onboarding and monthly churn falls to 3%. What is the lifetime value of a customer now?

distractors.note: the misconception: revenue instead of gross margin
a fixed one-year life, which cannot respond to a change in churn

far_transfer.text: A retailer's customers spend EUR 200 a year with it, the gross margin on that spending is 30%, and a customer shops with the retailer for five years on average. What is the lifetime value of a customer?

distractors.note: the misconception: lifetime revenue rather than lifetime margin
counting a single year of margin instead of the whole relationship
